   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From: F. Ferrari, LONDON

I have a Spectrum+2A and a SAM
which I use much more than the
Spectrum owing to the different
sizes of dumps you can get out
from the printer.

I have a Spectrum graphics prog-
ram which loads OK into the SAM
through the "SPECMAKER" soft-
ware, (incidentally that's how I
found out about yourselves
because it runs a program about
you on the disk) but it will
only print out a very small
picture. Is there any way I can
get different size dumps?
Any help you may offer would be
appreciated.
                     F. Ferrari


Brian Cavers to F. Ferrari

The "small picture" printed out
is due to the limitation of your
"Spectrum graphics program" and
obviously I can't say much more
about it because you don't say
what the program is!

Presumably your Spectrum graphic
program has a "SAVE SCREEN" so
the only alternative is to save
the screen to ramdisk then exit
back to SAM mode using MOVE 2
(this may be built in to your
graphic program already) and use
the save ramdisk option. At the
prompt "save all?" press N and
just enter the filename of the
screen when it asks. Now do the
following...

Remove the disc and reset your
computer and enter the following
few lines...

10 MODE 1
20 LET SC=((IN 252 BAND 31)+1)*
   16384 : REM SCREEN ADDRESS
30 LOAD "NAME%"CODE 98403
40 POKE SC,MEM$(98423 TO 105334)
50 SAVE "NAME2"SCREEN$

Note that the name in line 30 is
the filename you gave the screen
when saving it to the ramdisk
with "%" on the end. "NAME2" in
line 50 is any name you like so
long as it's different.

RUN the above and the screen is
now a Mode 1 SAM SCREEN$ which
you can load in FLASH and dump
or use the SAM DUMP routine.

When loading Mode 1 screens into
FLASH, always first select Mode
1 in the "MODE" menu and then
select "COLOUR OK" in the
"SCREEN" menu. If the screen is
still all "pink" after loading
the screen, select "SPEC.COL" in
the "SCREEN" menu. It may be
worth first changing the mode to
MODE 4 in the"MODES" menu before
dumping.

You can change the size of the
SAM DUMP by POKEing the SYSVARS
between 18 and 39 (see Page 176
of your SAM User's Guide.

It should be possible to put a
SAM Mode 1 screen in SPECMAKER.
Let me know if you want me to
try!
                      - Brian

From: Gordon Henderson, ABERDEEN

Thank you for solving my OUTDEX
problem. You were right, I had a
ROM 2. My original SAM was con-
verted to ROM 3 but it got a bug
somewhere else in its guts and
PBT could not cure it. I managed
to get another SAM without
drives or power supply and it
was the culprit with the ROM2. I
have now swapped the ROM's and
all is OK. Thanks again.

I purchased an OUTWRITE from
SAMCO for `17.00 without real-
ising I could have got it from
you for `12.00. I am, however,
very pleased with it, although I
would like adjustable margins
like TW.

My printer is a POLO Mark II
made by RADOFIN ELECTRONICS in
Hong-Kong. I got it in a package
when I bought my OPUS Discovery
some years ago from SAGA SYSTEMS
I have entered LC10 at option 8
of the OUTWRITE Menu and have
the use of Bold, Condensed,
Double Strike, Emphasised, NLQ,
Italics, Subscipt, Underline &
Double Width.

I also purchased 'The Style
Writer' but I find the printout
routine very slow and compli-
cated. This may be because its
colour and graphics capability
are too sophisticated for my
purposes.

        Gordon Henderson

Brian Cavers to Gordon Henderson

The new upgrade OUTWRITE will
have variable margins and you'll
be able to reform the text in
those margins whether you have
increased or decreased them. It
has a "cut and paste" feature
too so you can take a section of
text from anywhere and re-print
it anywhere else within whatever
margins are set.There'll be lots
more new features including much
improved printer features to
make it as easy as possible to
set up and to use.

STYLEWRITER does have a lot of
features and so takes longer to
get to grips with. The graphic
print inevitably takes longer.
                        - Brian

From: Malcolm Wright, CO. DURHAM

I used to have one of these
printers. It wasn't mine, just a
loan from a friend. What I used
to do was run it from my 48K
SPECCY using a KEMPSTON "E"
interface as this had the appro-
priate driver in ROM or rather
EPROM hence the name. I tried it
on the SAM and got various
strange results.

I now have an AMSTRAD DMP 2000,
and share an OLIVETTI DM124c
24-pin colour printer with my
brother.

You are correct in assuming that
CHR$ 0 is the escape code for
the GPA 100A.

It will work satisfactorily with
the SAM only if all driver soft-
ware is "custom" made. Spare
ribbons for this machine are
available cheaply from RIBBONS
DIRECT. I've lost their address
but a quick check in the trade
magzines will get you this. (See
my notes on re-inking later).

At one time SEIKOSHA made this
printer for TANDY under the
RADIO SHACK brand.An upgrade ROM
used to be available for the
printer to allow faster draft
speed and NLQ. These printers
were the mainstay of many an
office at one time but now, with
their odd standard parallel/
Centronics interface and non-NLQ
text they are a little anti-
quated.

Don't get me wrong - they are a
very good and robust printer if
you don't mind the limitations.

SEIKOSHA (SEIKO/EPSON) are a bit
"funny" to deal with when it
comes to after-sales service. If
you're not a BIG concern they
treat you with little respect.
So, if you have problems with
this or other SEIKOSHA printers,
don't say I didn't warn you.

On the subject of printers, any-
one who has problems with the
"muddy yellow" syndrome there is
a simple solution. Always remem-
ber the following golden rule:-

Dark TO light is never right,
Dark ON light is better.

I.e., print white, then yellow,
then cyan, then magenta and
lastly black. This way the
lighter inks don't pick up the
darker ones. It's easy when you
think about it.


I got the idea watching a four-
colour lithographic system in
use. It also applies to some
silk screen printing proccesses!


Now if only the chaps who write
printer drivers would learn this
rule I might not need to keep
buying expensive ribbons.

A little explaining of how my
BAR SCROLL [SAM OUTLET 52] works
would not go amiss here so....

M$ contains the message A$ is
the array which contains the
font LOGO$ contains my ZAEON
logo chr$ 13 (carriage return)
fast clear of text on bar chr$
129 bar wipe up/down chr$ 137
colour rotate chr$ 142 put my
logo in center of bar TASWORD
save its files as code so mem$
these out and remove all the
"padding" spaces and add a chr$
13 at the end of each line.

It's fairly simple to write a
routine to do this. You could
use other graphic chr$ to do
other fx if you like; I leave
that up to you.

Any reader can use the scroller
in his/her progs; just give me a
small mention.

The technique I used to wipe the
bar up and down in the LOGO DEMO
[OUTLET 50](yes,it DID only take
20 mins to write, I had some
routines in stock so to speak
from a simple SPECTRUM version)
was to OUT values from 0 to 191
into port 249.

A quick check in the SAM
TECHNICAL MANUAL will tell you
that this handles the line
position of a palette change in
palette 0. This makes a bouncing
horizon a breeze from BASIC just
try OUTing random values in this
can be hilarious.

Onto the subject of re-inking
(black!) ribbons. I have two
printers at my disposal normally
but one is out on loan. One is
an AMSTRRAD DMP2000 (same as the
3000 and 3160) and the other a
24 pin colour printer an
OLIVETTI DM124c.

I tend to re-ink my AMSTRAD
ribbons as these are the easiest
to get at. The mixture I have
found that works the best (some
dry up too quickly) is STEPHENS
endorsing or stamp pad ink,a
drop of washing-up liquid and a
drop or two of WD40 or TANDY's
RECISION OILER lubricant (this
is a TEFLON based liquid).
ALLWAYS SHAKE the mixture a
little before applying to the
ribbon.

In the case of my machine I
found that attaching a nozzle
from a used can of WD40 to the
ink bottle,which is plastic and
squeezy, I could apply the
mixture direct to the ribbon
without getting too messy.

Remember to put the printer into
self-test while doing this, and
let it run till the desired
quality of print is achieved
without getting the ribbon
totally drenched in ink.

The reason for the WD40 in the
mixture is purely to prevent the
ink clogging up the print head,
the washing-up liquid helps to
prevent the ink drying out too
quickly on the ribbon.

So far this has worked exceed-
ingly well. Other types of
ribbon may have to be done in a
different manner but if you use
the nozzle technique you don't
get yourself too dirty. I am not
sure if anyone makes yellow,
cyan or magenta stamp pad inks,
but if they do then I'll try
doing a colour ribbon next. I'll
let you know how I get on.

Thank you for producing the BEST
mag around for BOTH the SAM and
SPECTRUM.

         Malcolm Wright

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Wright

Thanks, Malcolm. Your VALLEY OF
ADVENTURE role-playing game is
now planned for next month's
OUTLET on both SAM and Spectrum!

Thanks for all the other info
although I must make the usual -
CHEZRON accept no responsibility
etc. clause for your re-inking
method. The bubbles may tend to
get up one's nose.

                    Brian

From: D. Wornham, DROITWICH SPA

     TEACHER'S PET SOFTWARE
       REVIEW - OUTLET 53

Whilst agreeing with the
principle that reviews should be
honest and fair I am writing to
express my unease at the
impression given by Brian Gaff's
review of Teacher's Pet educat-
ional software in OUTLET 53.

I am not a teacher or a child of
primary school age, towards whom
these programs are aimed (e.g.
P7-9 on the T.P. lists means
Primary School age 7 to 9 years)
but had the opportunity to try a
selection of T.P. programs when
my children were near that age
and they used the programs.

I do not disagree with Brian's
summary of the programs and know
that Keith Pirie welcomes
comments, so 'the small range of
countries' in "Countries and
Capitals" repeated questions in
"Euro Trivia" the ability to
cheat by using ESC and typing in
the sum rather than the calcul-
ated answer in "Pop Star" will,
no doubt, motivate the author to
suitably modify the programs -
an admirable aim for reviewers.

Commenting that a Clip Art Demo.
is "good fun but little else"
surely misses the point that
such pictures are intended to be
entered into a collection for
use within programs, screen$,
desk top publications, etc. when
needed!

He omits to mention the quality,
price and subject variety.

We are not informed whether the
reviewer has the experience of a
teacher or parent of young
children or if he has had the
benefit of observing children
using these programs and hearing
their comments.

There is no comparison of their
cost and value to the few other
educational games available for
the SAM and Spectrum, such as
those from Leo Software, 25,
Chatsworth Gardens, Scarborough,
North Yorkshire, YO12 7NQ.

I do know that primary teachers
have been consulted before and

during the writing of Teacher's
Pet progs., that my children
have enjoyed their use and that
they are good value with special
offers for combinations of
programs.

Those of us who are regular
computer users must, surely,
beware the danger of comparing
impressive, expensive, high
quality games with fancy, often
animated, screen$, which can
have limited educational value,
to those produced to educate at
home and school.

Whilst it would be great to have
educational programs of this
standard they will be expensive,
e.g. "5 on a Treasure Island" at

`14.99 - and that, I suspect -
having only seen it used by
another - is only "educational"
by use of logic, spelling and
typing they need not be so -
they need simplicity of use as
initially the children, parents
and teachers often have no
previous computer experience.

They do not need impressive
pictures to be fun to use and
provide education and a large
collection of economical prog-
rams, even if each provides only
a short attention span, must
surely be better than a few
expensive ones.

Despite being generally low in
price, educational programs are,

unfortunately, not generally
commercially viable to produce
for the SAM and Spectrum as the
Acorn Computers' BBC, Master and
Archimedes have cornered most of
the educational market so we
must do all we can to encourage
such programs with any comments
being realistic and constructive
or we run the risk of discour-
aging those few who are trying
to help the Spectrum and SAM
achieve their undoubted potent-
ial in the the educational
market.

How about a reader with children
or pupils of Primary School age
sending for a selection of
Teacher's Pet and Leo Software
programs, (they may get them

free if the purpose is stated)
observing the children with them
and then submitting a joint
report on their comparative
fun/interest/education/value?I'm
sure that OUTLET will pay hand-
somely (?) for such a project.

        Yours Sincerely,

          David Wornham

Brian Cavers to David Wornham

I re-read Brian Gaff's review
and it looks fair to me.

I agree that all reviews should
have the price and we try to
always include it but often
software is sent to us without
the price! I do not have the
software and its accompanying
literature at hand but it may be
that it wasn't clear as to the
target age group (in fact, Brian
does say "I am not sure who
these programs are aimed at").

Again, I do not have the soft-
ware at hand but I think it just
had the clip art demo added on
without comment as to its use?

Is the clip art really appropri-
ate in an educational program?

It can be taken as read that if
a reviewer doesn't SAY he has
had the experiences of a teacher
or parent or child to draw on
then he has NOT - so the review
can be read as the point of view
of just that person.

I'm all for encouraging people
to write software - especially
in a minority market but not at
the expense of truth and if a
reviewer gives his honest
opinion then that is all I ask.
As repeatedly stated in OUTLET,
I would much prefer to receive
two or three reviews of the same
software from different people
so that we do get a varied view.

Your own letter helps to put a
different light on the review
and is most welcome for that
reason but I do think it falsely
implies that Brian Gaff's review
was highly critical whereas it
was light in tone and mostly
favourable.He only sums up with
the comment that it may have a
limited life with the children
of today which may be true.

I would certainly welcome any
further reports along the lines
you suggest - i.e., influenced
by direct observations of the
software being used by children
(Yes, we do pay for articles!).
However, given the software to
review, I think Brian Gaff gave
a fair assessment as he saw it.
                        - Brian

From: Mike Pike, NORTHALLERTON

This is just a note on the sub-
ject of sending disks and other
magnetic material through the
post.I have sent disks and tapes
through the post many times, as
well as having received them.
Sometimes, the disks can get
corrupted in the post,as someone
mentioned in a recent letter.

I know this because I have test-
ed disks before sending them and
they can still arrive corrupted
at the other end.

However, I have had no problems
(so far) with cassettes. I think
this has something to do with
the way the information is
stored.

For example, normal IBM 5.25"
360k disks were the only disks
to survive when I recently had a
parcel of disks sent to me. The
1.2Mb 5.25" disks were all
corrupted in some way.

All the cassettes I have sent
and received in the post have
been OK as well. This could be
because the information is
stored in narrow tracks on 3.5"
and high density 5.25" disks.


The 360k 5.25" disk uses a wider
recording strip, as does a
normal cassette tape. So what
can you do to protect your data?
ALWAYS make sure you have a
backup copy before posting.

Sending data on cassette rather
than disk sounds a good idea,
but it usually inconveniences
both parties.

Don't rely on a label on your
letter such as"MAGNETIC MEDIA"or
somesuch. These markings(includ-
ing "FRAGILE") can't be seen
when the item is upside-down or
at the bottom of a postbag.

There is no substitute for care-
ful packaging: You can prevent
some of the stray magnetic
fields reaching your disks by
lining your Outlet wallet with
kitchen foil. If you send disks
on their own, try just wrapping
the disk, or make your own card-
board wallet.

For the physicists among you,
this creates a Faraday Cage, so
magnetic energy travels around
the outside of the tinfoil
rather than straight through the
disk. That's the theory anyway!

You can get special disk-mailers
but these are usually just a
cardboard wallet lined with some
kind of material which does the
same job as the tinfoil.

These ideas only cost a few
pence so why not give them a
try? They are not 100 percent
guaranteed but they may well
stop some of your disks being
corrupted.
            Mike Pike
                        more...

PS.The Post Office's recommend-
ation (in their leaflet "Wrap Up
Well") is to use a box with at
least 4 inches of soft packing
all around!
               Mike Pike
.

To Mike Pike from Brian Gaff

Well, we send many discs through
the post and very few are
returned as faulty. The most
common problem is drives that
are slightly out of alignment.

A magazine did some tests on
corruption a few years ago. The
only postal corruption they had
was traced to the disc being
close to a motor in a train. The
A/C field can be quite strong,
as you can imagine.

By the way, as an aside, never
put a floppy on top of a CD
player, as many have large
permanent magnets in the disc
clamp!               - B.G.

From: Malcolm Goodman, LEEDS


Brian/Ron

This may be 'old hat' but since
I don't have any SAM-specific
copies of OUTLET I write anyway.

Being new to the SAM computer,
one of the first things I did
was get it working like a
Spectrum. Further examination of
the paging code made me aware
that it should be possible to
put a copy of the Spectrum ROM
at address 0 but with the
ability to poke, and alter, any
ROM addresses. I, therefore,
tried this out and found that
indeed it did work.

However, in the process I
discovered that data corruption
occured in the character set and
also in locations 0 to 4, and
this warranted investigation.

The offending bits of code
reside at locations 3372 and
13308/9.

The solution was quite simple.

Firstly, load a copy of the
Spectrum's ROM into the SAM at
65536.

Then 'POKE 68908,23', DPOKE
78844,19

Next enter the following code in
line 9999:-

POKE 50000,1250,35,237,65,1,252,
4,237,65,199: CALL 50000

In a few moments your SAM
becomes a Spectrum and you can
alter ROM addresses to your
heart's content.

One small restriction: don't try
putting anything into locations
19 to 23 inclusive as these will
be altered as the Spectrum runs.

Apart from this you can now POKE
to ROM addresses to see what
results.

NOW HERE'S A ROUTINE FOR THE
SPECTRUM WHICH MAY BE OF
INTEREST...

On the SAM there is a command
'INPUT #2;"name";a$', which
results in the prompt appearing
on the upper screen. Well, now
we can have something comparable
for the Spectrum. I've done it
all in BASIC so that more users
can see what's happening...

10 LET a=PEEK 23631+256*peek
23632.

20 POKE a+7,168: POKE a+8,16

30 INPUT#2;"name ";#0;a$: PRINT
a$

40 INPUT#2;"age ";#0;b$:PRINT b$

50 INPUT#2;"sex ";#0;c$:PRINT c$
and so on.

As you will see, if you run
this, the prompt will appear on
the upper screen. Your response
will be entered on the lower
screen and will then be printed
in the upper screen adjacent to
the prompt.

An excellent way of entering
multiple inputs.

You could try omitting the #0 in
these lines but the results get
very messy and need lots of ''''
to tidy it up. you also get lots
of cursors printed !!.

           Malcolm Goodman

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Goodman

Thanks, Malcolm. I shall have to
experiment a bit with that input
routine.

As for Spectrum emulators on the
SAM, there are numerous ones (we
have had two in OUTLET) but it's
interesting to see it presented
in this way. What fascinated me
here is this corruption. The
reason why I think nobody(?) has
been aware of this is that it is
possible on the SAM to "WRITE
PROTECT" the RAM in the first
page so that even machine code
cannot write to it. This is done
by setting bit 7 of the low
memory page register (port 250).
                        - Brian

From:Malcolm Perry,KIDDERMINSTER

Dear Brian and Ron,

I recently wrote in and mention-
ed that I was missing the "DISC
WRITE PROTECTED" error report.
This has been put down simply to
the way the SYS was set up and I
have not made any effort so far
to correct it.

However, when I formatted some
discs that according to SAM had
all been "OK" on verify but when
I came to use them found that in
fact the disc was full of the
old data and the verify had
passed simply because the old
format was intact - I decided it
was time to look into things.

Hunting through all the manuals
I could find no reference to
turning on and off this error
report. Doing an "on error" and
printing the error code proved
it was not getting the error
report for "write protect".

Further investigation proved it
was only drive 1 that was at
fault - drive 2 acted normally.
I could think of no reason why
this should be so and changed
over drives. Guess what this
problem turns out to be?  A
faulty drive. I presume while
the write protect is working
within the drive as it is not
actually writing, this inform-
ation is not getting back into
SAM so it assumes all is normal
and proceeds accordingly.

So once again it looks like a
drive back to SAMCO. The last
one went back twice and took 3
months or so. I wonder how long
this will take to sort out.

Now, can I ask,through OUTLET,if
other readers have had any
problems with their new SAMS. It
seems strange I should have 3
SAMs that one way or another
have had faults.

The previous two were sent back
as unacceptable and this third
came with two faults in the PSU
and it seems two faulty drives.

As a friend of mine said "It
can't only be you that are
having these problems".

So all I'd like to know from SAM
users is "have you had any
problems with your new SAM" so I
can put things into proportion.

If you include your name and
address it will be kept in
confidence but if you wish just
use initials,say, and town or
post code or nothing!

At the moment all I am inter-
ested in is some idea of scale
of problems or if they even
exist. Perhaps it is just that I
have received the only 3 SAMs
with faults, the only 2 PSU with
poor soldering and damaged
component, the only 2 drives
that have not been satisfactory
out of all the SAMS
manufactured.

Perhaps having a technical
background is a disadvantage?
Maybe if I did not have I would
simply put the faults down to
the "normal" way things work.


Perhaps in some cases faults
exist but the user does not
realise. Like my missing "write
protected". At first I simply
passed it off as "the way the
system works".


If a drive fails to format discs
it is probably put down to "bad
discs" but is it? My replacement
drive works fine with previous
drives rejections as"bad discs".
How is the average user to know?

If, as with the PSUs where two
had a component not soldered and
the video to TV was missing or
went on and off if the PSU
moved, then it is more obvious.
It is obviously noticeable if
you get a PSU with a spare nut
rattling around inside. I found
its associated screw loose in
the packing.


If it is a poor sound or picture
and you are told it may be your
TV and a monitor works better -
who is to argue unless you are
in a position to prove other-
wise? One of mine was an out of
tune modulator in PSU I guess as
the second and third was OK on
same TV.

If your SAM refuses to load from
your recorder and you are told
it is probably your recorder who
is to argue?

It is interesting though that
the 2nd and 3rd SAMs work OK
with the same recorder and that
the first SAM refused to do so.

         Malcolm Perry,

         216,Marlpool Lane,
         Kidderminster,
         Worcs. DY11 5DL

Brian Cavers to Malcom Perry

We've had direct contact with
six SAMs and seven or eight

The "small picture" printed out is due to the limitation of your "Spectrum graphics program" and obviously I can't say much more about it because you don't say what the program is!

Presumably your Spectrum graphic program has a "SAVE SCREEN" so the only alternative is to save the screen to ramdisk then exit back to SAM mode using MOVE 2 (this may be built in to your graphic program already) and use the save ramdisk option. At the prompt "save all?" press N and just enter the filename of the screen when it asks. Now do the following...

Remove the disc and reset your computer and enter the following few lines...

10 MODE 1 20 LET SC=((IN 252 BAND 31)+1)* 16384 : REM SCREEN ADDRESS 30 LOAD "NAME%"CODE 98403 40 POKE SC,MEM$(98423 TO 105334) 50 SAVE "NAME2"SCREEN$

Note that the name in line 30 is the filename you gave the screen when saving it to the ramdisk with "%" on the end. "NAME2" in line 50 is any name you like so long as it's different.

RUN the above and the screen is now a Mode 1 SAM SCREEN$ which you can load in FLASH and dump or use the SAM DUMP routine.

When loading Mode 1 screens into FLASH, always first select Mode 1 in the "MODE" menu and then select "COLOUR OK" in the "SCREEN" menu. Dark TO light is never right, Dark ON light is better.

I.e., print white, then yellow, then cyan, then magenta and lastly black. This way the lighter inks don't pick up the darker ones. It's easy when you think about it.

This is just a note on the sub- ject of sending disks and other magnetic material through the post.I have sent disks and tapes through the post many times, as well as having received them. Sometimes, the disks can get corrupted in the post,as someone mentioned in a recent letter.

Don't rely on a label on your letter such as"MAGNETIC MEDIA"or somesuch. These markings(includ- ing "FRAGILE") can't be seen when the item is upside-down or at the bottom of a postbag.

There is no substitute for care- ful packaging: You can prevent some of the stray magnetic fields reaching your disks by lining your Outlet wallet with kitchen foil. If you send disks on their own, try just wrapping the disk, or make your own card- board wallet.

For the physicists among you, this creates a Faraday Cage, so magnetic energy travels around the outside of the tinfoil rather than straight through the disk. That's the theory anyway!

You can get special disk-mailers but these are usually just a cardboard wallet lined with some kind of material which does the same job as the tinfoil.

These ideas only cost a few pence so why not give them a try? They are not 100 percent guaranteed but they may well stop some of your disks being corrupted. Mike Pike

This may be 'old hat' but since I don't have any SAM-specific copies of OUTLET I write anyway.

Being new to the SAM computer, one of the first things I did was get it working like a Spectrum. Further examination of the paging code made me aware that it should be possible to put a copy of the Spectrum ROM at address 0 but with the ability to poke, and alter, any ROM addresses. I, therefore, tried this out and found that indeed it did work.

However, in the process I discovered that data corruption occured in the character set and also in locations 0 to 4, and this warranted investigation.

The offending bits of code reside at locations 3372 and 13308/9.

The solution was quite simple.

Firstly, load a copy of the Spectrum's ROM into the SAM at 65536.

Then 'POKE 68908,23', DPOKE 78844,19

Next enter the following code in line 9999:-

```text
POKE 50000,1250,35,237,65,1,252,
4,237,65,199: CALL 50000
```

In a few moments your SAM becomes a Spectrum and you can alter ROM addresses to your heart's content.

One small restriction: don't try putting anything into locations 19 to 23 inclusive as these will be altered as the Spectrum runs.

Apart from this you can now POKE to ROM addresses to see what results.

NOW HERE'S A ROUTINE FOR THE SPECTRUM WHICH MAY BE OF INTEREST...

On the SAM there is a command 'INPUT #2;"name";a$', which results in the prompt appearing on the upper screen. Well, now we can have something comparable for the Spectrum. I've done it all in BASIC so that more users can see what's happening...

10 LET a=PEEK 23631+256*peek 23632.

20 POKE a+7,168: POKE a+8,16

30 INPUT#2;"name ";#0;a$: PRINT a$

40 INPUT#2;"age ";#0;b$:PRINT b$

50 INPUT#2;"sex ";#0;c$:PRINT c$ and so on.

As you will see, if you run this, the prompt will appear on the upper screen. Your response will be entered on the lower screen and will then be printed in the upper screen adjacent to the prompt.

An excellent way of entering multiple inputs.

You could try omitting the #0 in these lines but the results get very messy and need lots of '''' to tidy it up. you also get lots of cursors printed !!.

Malcolm Goodman

```text
10 MODE 1
20 LET SC=((IN 252 BAND 31)+1)*16384 : REM SCREEN ADDRESS
30 LOAD "NAME%"CODE 98403
40 POKE SC,MEM$(98423 TO 105334)
50 SAVE "NAME2"SCREEN$
```

Обратите внимание, что имя в строке 30 — это имя файла, которое вы дали экрану при сохранении его на рамдиск, со знаком «%» на конце. «NAME2» в строке 50 — любое имя по вашему вкусу, главное, чтобы оно отличалось.

Вы можете изменить размер SAM DUMP, изменяя значения системных переменных (SYSVARS) с помощью POKE от 18 до 39 (см. стр. 176 вашего SAM User's Guide).

Темное К светлому — плохой совет,  
Темное НА светлое — вот ответ.

То есть сначала печатайте белым, затем желтым, потом голубым (cyan), потом пурпурным (magenta) и напоследок черным. Таким образом, более светлые чернила не будут пачкаться о темные. Все просто, если подумать.

Эти идеи стоят всего несколько пенсов, так почему бы не попробовать? Они не дают стопроцентной гарантии, но вполне могут спасти некоторые ваши диски от повреждения.

Дальнейшее изучение кода переключения страниц навело меня на мысль, что должна быть возможность поместить копию ROM Спектрума по адресу 0, но с возможностью изменять (через POKE) любые адреса этого ROM. Я попробовал реализовать это, и всё действительно заработало.

Однако в процессе я обнаружил, что происходит повреждение данных в наборе символов, а также в ячейках с 0 по 4, что потребовало расследования.

Виновные участки кода находились по адресам 3372 и 13308/9.

Решение оказалось довольно простым.

Во-первых, загрузите копию ROM Спектрума в SAM по адресу 65536.

Затем выполните:
```text
POKE 68908,23 : DPOKE 78844,19
```

Затем введите следующий код в строку 9999:
```text
POKE 50000,1250,35,237,65,1,252,4,237,65,199: CALL 50000
```

Через пару мгновений ваш SAM превратится в Spectrum, и вы сможете менять адреса ROM сколько душе угодно.

Одно небольшое ограничение: не пытайтесь ничего записывать в адреса с 19 по 23 включительно, так как они изменяются во время работы Спектрума.

В остальном теперь вы можете применять POKE к адресам ROM и смотреть, что получится.

А ТЕПЕРЬ ПРОЦЕДУРА ДЛЯ SPECTRUM, КОТОРАЯ МОЖЕТ ОКАЗАТЬСЯ ПОЛЕЗНОЙ...

На SAM есть команда:
```text
INPUT #2;"name";a$
```
в результате чего запрос появляется на верхнем экране. Что ж, теперь у нас есть нечто подобное и для Spectrum. Я написал всё на Бейсике, чтобы большему числу пользователей было понятно, что происходит:

```text
10 LET a=PEEK 23631+256*peek 23632
20 POKE a+7,168: POKE a+8,16
30 INPUT#2;"name ";#0;a$: PRINT a$
40 INPUT#2;"age ";#0;b$:PRINT b$
50 INPUT#2;"sex ";#0;c$:PRINT c$
```
и так далее.

Как вы увидите при запуске, приглашение ко вводу появится на верхнем экране. Ваш ответ будет набираться на нижнем экране, а затем напечатается на верхнем рядом с приглашением.

Отличный способ для организации множественного ввода данных.

Вы можете попробовать убрать `#0` в этих строках, но результат станет очень неаккуратным и потребует множества `'''` для очистки; к тому же будет печататься куча курсоров!!
